sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reread Lock-based isolation levels and Row-versioning isolation levels: READ UNCOMMITTED permits dirty observations, SERIALIZABLE protects read ranges, RCSI reads a statement snapshot, and SNAPSHOT supplies a consistent view across statements. The enabling database option and explicit session selection are documented; universal no-blocking language is not accepted.

The actual product text dates row-versioned READ COMMITTED and SNAPSHOT to SQL Server 2005, distinguishes their version-selection boundaries and places the XSN at first data access. SERIALIZABLE retains data/range locks; versioned reads still acquire Sch-S and can encounter Sch-M contention. These sections independently bound the repaired question.

choiceReviews.rationale: Consider a commit after the first SELECT and before the next. RCSI can use that newer committed version for the next statement even inside the same explicit transaction. That is useful when each statement should see fresh committed data, but it cannot guarantee this report's common transaction-wide view.

SERIALIZABLE can keep the read set consistent by retaining shared and applicable range locks, but that prevents conflicting updates from freely committing and does not provide the requested versioned read view. It would fit a requirement that accepts this locking to enforce serialization, not both conditions in the stem.

With ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION enabled and the session using SNAPSHOT, successive reads use the transaction's version-selection boundary rather than resampling at each statement. Ordinary row writers are not blocked by shared data-read locks. First data access establishes the snapshot; schema-lock and update-conflict exceptions are not being denied.

READ UNCOMMITTED can observe an uncommitted writer's value that is later rolled back, as well as changing values across reads. Avoiding shared read locks does not make those observations a stable committed snapshot. Only a task explicitly tolerating such inconsistency could use that trade-off.

sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Reread Modify data without optimized locking: a SNAPSHOT update detects an intervening committed row modification and terminates the conflicting transaction. Applications must handle and retry those conflicts, including the noted constraint/indexed-view cases. The optimized-locking section preserves this SNAPSHOT rule rather than granting RCSI's automatic retry behavior.

The SNAPSHOT discussion confirms stable reads do not authorize silently overwriting a competing write. A business operation that reads, calculates and writes depends on the read value; the isolation setting does not independently validate a calculation reused after a conflict. The unit's flawed overselling illustration is not treated as a proof.

choiceReviews.rationale: The conflict invalidates the old transaction. Repeating the complete read-calculate-write operation in a new snapshot rechecks the debit against the changed balance instead of transporting a stale result. The absence of external effects and permission for bounded retries make this a valid recovery strategy, not a guarantee every retry will succeed.

The other writer has already committed, and the first transaction encountered a terminating snapshot conflict. There is no still-valid failed transaction to resume merely by waiting. Waiting would address an active lock owner before ordinary blocking ends; it cannot undo this abort or validate the old computed value.

Opening a new transaction does not refresh the balance used in the old absolute UPDATE result. Such a value could erase the effect of the concurrent transaction, for example an intervening credit. A newly validated conditional/idempotent operation would require a different contract; this option explicitly skips the necessary reread.

Conflict detection reports that this write attempt cannot complete under its snapshot; it is not a successful concurrency-validation result. A transaction whose update validation succeeds can commit, but the described terminated attempt has no accepted original debit to commit.

Check currently executing queries describes active requests and blocking_session_id, while the sessions/waiting-tasks section provides the broader session view. Execution plans and missing-index analysis can identify access-path improvements. None of that equates an absent active request with a session having released its transaction resources.

Code guidelines recommend short transactions and accessing less data to reduce contention. Discover long-running transactions identifies transaction inspection and owner tracing for appropriate commit/rollback; Terminate a transaction warns to use KILL carefully. These bound the recommended owner-coordinated investigation instead of authorizing automatic termination.

choiceReviews.rationale: Testing an index can be sensible when a statement's broad access path causes long lock retention. Here request 61 is the downstream waiter on 58. Improving 61's possible future footprint does not first locate the still-open transaction upstream of both wait edges.

A narrower UPDATE or shorter batches can reduce transaction duration and contention when that transaction is the relevant lock holder. Session 58 is also waiting on 52, so choosing it merely because it blocks 61 stops the investigation too early. Its batch design may be reviewed later, after locating the upstream transaction.

system_health deadlock reports are a real SQL Server diagnostic, and a recorded victim can require recovery. The supplied evidence is a live wait chain reaching a sleeping session with an open transaction, not a report establishing a victim for this incident. Historical deadlock investigation is therefore not the first way to locate this open transaction.

Following 61 -> 58 -> 52 identifies the upstream session whose open transaction should be inspected first. Sleeping and having no active request do not mean its transaction ended. Coordinating with the application owner supports authorized completion or rollback after inspection, not an automatic commit, KILL or claim that every relevant lock has already been proven.
